narrator.instruct: Gripping, energetic storyteller telling a true invention story with a funny twist, brisk, excited and punchy, never calm.

colleague.instruct: A young engineer in 1945 jumping back as an egg explodes next to him, startled and half laughing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The story goes, this man's candy bar melted in his pocket, and nothing in the room was hot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His name was Percy Spencer. He never finished grammar school, and taught himself the science from books.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In the war he worked on radar tubes called magnetrons. His method made two thousand six hundred a day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But standing next to a running magnetron, he found sticky chocolate all over his pocket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He grabbed raw popcorn kernels and held them by the tube. They popped all over the lab.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Next, an egg in a kettle. It shook, and then it burst.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So how does a radar tube cook without any fire?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You see, the tube sends out microwaves. They make the water inside food twist back and forth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: All that rubbing between molecules turns into heat, right inside the food. No flame at all.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: On October eighth, nineteen forty-five, a patent was filed for cooking with microwaves.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The first oven, in nineteen forty-seven, stood six feet tall and weighed seven hundred and fifty pounds.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Twenty years later, in nineteen sixty-seven, a countertop model cost four hundred ninety-five dollars.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So every bag of microwave popcorn goes back to one melted candy bar.
